lead: Blockchain is a shared ledger that many parties keep in step without a single owner. It exists because digital cash kept failing at one problem: a file can be copied, so one coin could be spent twice. The 2008 Bitcoin design solved that, and the ledger idea inside it outgrew the currency. Today the same idea sits behind cross-border payments, supply-chain records, land registries and smart contracts. This chapter traces how it got here: pre-Bitcoin digital cash, the 2008 whitepaper, the 2009 genesis block, Ethereum in 2015, and enterprise ledgers after that.
prereq: You need: no earlier chapter; a rough idea of a database helps, and hashing is covered later (see Unit 2, Cryptographic hash functions and SHA-256).

blocks.text: Money stored as bits can be copied perfectly and free. A paper note cannot be in two places at once; a file can. If a buyer sends the same digital coin to two sellers, both see a payment that looks valid. This is double spending, and every digital-cash design before 2008 had to answer it.

Most answers used a central party. In the 1980s David Chaum's ecash hid buyer identity behind blind signatures, but a bank still cleared each coin to stop reuse. Later proposals such as b-money, bit gold and hashcash (proof of work used to price email) supplied pieces of a system, not a whole one.
A working system needed two things at once:

items: No central issuer, so no single party can freeze or inflate the money.
One agreed history, so every participant accepts the same order of transactions.

blocks.text: The second is the hard part, and it is a consensus problem; see Unit 3, Consensus mechanisms and their types. The building blocks were already known: hash functions and hash pointers (Unit 2, Linking blocks with hash pointers), Merkle trees, and digital signatures. Nobody had assembled them into a ledger that a stranger could verify. That assembly is what 2008 delivered.

sections.h3: The 2008 whitepaper and the 2009 genesis block

blocks.text: In October 2008 a short paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System appeared online. Its author is credited as Satoshi Nakamoto, a pseudonym; the real identity has never been confirmed. The claim was narrow and strong: payments between strangers, with no trusted third party, over a peer-to-peer network.

The method in outline: transactions are broadcast to the network, nodes gather them into a block, each block carries the hash of the block before it, producing a block costs computational work, and nodes follow the chain that has the most work behind it. Tampering with an old block breaks every link after it.

On 3 January 2009 the network produced its first block, the genesis block (block 0). It has no parent, so its previous-hash field is set to zero. It carried a 50 BTC coinbase reward. The first transfer to another person followed within days, and the ledger has run without an administrator since. That continuity is the real achievement of the genesis block.

Blockchain, defined separately: an ordered, append-only list of blocks, each block carrying the hash of its predecessor, copied across many nodes that accept a new block only if it obeys shared rules. Bitcoin is not the same thing. Bitcoin is a currency, a network and a protocol; blockchain is the ledger structure and update rule inside it. Think of blockchain as the notebook and Bitcoin as one account book written in it. Many blockchains now exist that hold no money at all (see 1.5).
Growth is usually told as three loose waves. The 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 numbering comes from industry writing, not a standards body; some syllabi call this the growth of blockchain technology.

Blockchain 1.0, currency. From 2009 Bitcoin showed the ledger worked at public scale. Altcoins copied the code with small changes: Namecoin for names, Litecoin for faster blocks (Unit 4, Alternative coins).

Blockchain 2.0, contracts. The Ethereum network launched in 2015, from a design proposed in 2013 by Vitalik Buterin and co-founders. It adds a virtual machine, so the ledger can run small programs. A smart contract is code stored on the chain that executes when its conditions are met, like a vending machine built in software (Unit 5, Smart contracts: concept and development). Ethereum also made issuing tokens a few lines of code.

Blockchain 3.0, wider use. Organisations that do not fully trust each other, but do know each other's identity, built consortium chains: a fixed set of validators rather than open membership. Hyperledger Fabric and Corda target trade finance, supply chain and insurance (Unit 6, Enterprise blockchain).

items: Scaling debates: bigger blocks versus layers above the chain. Disagreement produced hard forks such as Bitcoin Cash in 2017 (Unit 3, Forks).
Consortium and private chains: proof that the ledger idea was separated from a traded currency.

blocks.text: Both point to the same shift: blockchain outgrew digital cash and became a general way to keep a shared record.

figure.caption: The three dates students mix up, on one line: the 2008 whitepaper, the 2009 genesis block and the 2015 Ethereum launch. Blockchain did not begin in 2015; that launch came 7 years after the whitepaper.

examples.question: A student writes: 'Blockchain began in 2015 when Ethereum launched, and Bitcoin is the same thing as blockchain.' (a) Correct the statement using three well-known dates. (b) How many years separate the Bitcoin whitepaper from the Ethereum launch? (c) State the relation between Bitcoin and blockchain.
steps: Bitcoin whitepaper: October 2008, credited to Satoshi Nakamoto (a pseudonym).
Bitcoin genesis block: 3 January 2009. This is when the ledger actually started running.
Ethereum network launch: 2015. It is the first widely used blockchain with a built-in virtual machine for smart contracts.
Earliest of the three is 2008, so blockchain as a working system starts in 2008 to 2009, not 2015. Part (a) is corrected.
Whitepaper to Ethereum launch: 2015 minus 2008 = 7 years.
Whitepaper to genesis block: 2009 minus 2008 = 1 year.
Part (c): Bitcoin is one application built on the blockchain ledger idea; it is not identical to it.
examples.answer: Blockchain history starts with the 2008 whitepaper; the genesis block followed 1 year later in 2009, and Ethereum's 2015 launch came 7 years after the whitepaper. Bitcoin is one application of blockchain, not the same thing.

examples.question: A report says 'blockchain was invented when Ethereum launched in 2015'. Name two earlier milestones and give the year gap between the Bitcoin genesis block (3 January 2009) and the Ethereum launch (2015).
steps: Earlier milestone 1: the Bitcoin whitepaper, October 2008.
Earlier milestone 2: the Bitcoin genesis block, 3 January 2009.
Gap from genesis to Ethereum: 2015 minus 2009 = 6 years.
examples.answer: The whitepaper (2008) and the genesis block (2009) both precede Ethereum; the genesis block is 6 years before the 2015 launch.

traps: Writing 'Bitcoin and blockchain are the same'. Bitcoin is one currency and network; blockchain is the ledger structure and rules it uses.
Dating the start of Bitcoin to October 2008. That is the whitepaper; the network and its genesis block came on 3 January 2009.
Starting blockchain history at Ethereum in 2015, which skips roughly seven years of working Bitcoin history.
Treating a hard fork such as Bitcoin Cash as a software bug. It is a rule disagreement about block size that split the chain.
Assuming the 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 labels are official standards. They are informal industry labels for currency, contracts and wider enterprise use.

quiz.q: In which year was the Bitcoin whitepaper published, and who is credited as its author?
quiz.a: October 2008; Satoshi Nakamoto, a pseudonym whose real identity is unconfirmed.

quiz.q: What is the genesis block of Bitcoin, and what is special about its previous-hash field?
quiz.a: The first block of the Bitcoin chain, created 3 January 2009. It has no parent block, so its previous-hash field is set to zero.

quiz.q: Why does the ability to copy a file create the double-spending problem in digital cash?
quiz.a: A digital coin is data, so the same coin file can be sent to two different receivers. Without a shared record of spending order, both receivers treat the payment as valid.

quiz.q: Distinguish Bitcoin from blockchain in two sentences.
quiz.a: Blockchain is an append-only chain of blocks linked by hashes and copied across nodes that validate it by shared rules. Bitcoin is one currency and network that uses such a chain, not the chain idea itself.

quiz.q: A slide says 'blockchain arrived in 2015 with Ethereum'. Using the 2008 whitepaper and the 2009 genesis block, correct it and state the year gap between the genesis block and Ethereum.
quiz.a: Corrected: the idea is published in 2008 and runs live from 3 January 2009, so 2015 is not the start. Gap = 2015 minus 2009 = 6 years.

quiz.q: Why could digital signatures alone not replace a bank in digital cash, while signatures plus proof of work in a chain could?
quiz.a: A signature proves who authorised a payment but says nothing about order, so the same signed coin can be signed again for a second receiver. Proof of work plus a chained, replicated ledger fixes one global order of blocks, so nodes can reject the reused coin.

quiz.q: What does the rise of consortium chains suggest about the relation between blockchain and cryptocurrency?
quiz.a: That the shared-ledger mechanism is useful with no open currency at all. Known validators replace open mining, so blockchain is separable from cryptocurrency, though trust assumptions change.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now prefers the term DLT, distributed ledger technology, for permissioned systems where no coin is involved. Current work sits in layer-2 scaling, zero-knowledge proofs for privacy, and central bank digital currency pilots. Ethereum's own design documents are public and readable once you finish Unit 5. If you want to follow this further, search for the Bitcoin whitepaper, the Ethereum yellow paper, Hyperledger Fabric architecture, and CBDC pilot reports.
